title: Locks (L1)
scopeHtml: Scope: synchronized and monitors, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, StampedLock, lock granularity and ordering, and the coordination utilities (Semaphore, CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Phaser).

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does synchronized lock on, and what is the difference between a synchronized instance method, a static synchronized method, and a synchronized block?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know a lock is always tied to an object, not to code. Most "I synchronized it but it still races" bugs come from locking on different objects.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every Java object has an intrinsic lock, called its monitor. A synchronized instance method locks on this, a static synchronized method locks on the Class object, and a synchronized block locks on whatever object I name. Two threads exclude each other only if they lock the same object. The lock is reentrant, and entering and leaving also gives me happens-before visibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A monitor is a mutual-exclusion lock plus a wait set. Entering synchronized(x) means: acquire the monitor of x (blocking if another thread owns it), run the body, release on exit, including exit by exception. The JVM emits monitorenter/monitorexit bytecodes for blocks; for synchronized methods it sets the ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag instead.

instance method   synchronized void f()          lock = this
static method     static synchronized void g()   lock = Foo.class
block             synchronized (lockObj) {...}   lock = lockObj

Consequences:

  • f() on instance A and f() on instance B do not exclude each other (different this). A static synchronized method and an instance synchronized method also do not exclude each other (Foo.class vs this).
  • Reentrancy: the owner thread can re-enter; the monitor keeps a recursion count. So a synchronized method may call another synchronized method on the same object without deadlocking itself.
  • Memory semantics: unlock happens-before every later lock of the same monitor, so writes inside the block are visible to the next thread that locks it.
  • Prefer a private final lock object over this: outside code can also synchronized(yourObject) and interfere with, or deadlock, your internals.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Counter {
    private int n;
    private final Object lock = new Object(); // private: nobody else can lock on it

    void inc() { synchronized (lock) { n++; } }

    // BROKEN: locks on a String literal, which is interned and shared JVM-wide
    void bad() { synchronized ("lock") { n++; } }

    // BROKEN: each call creates a new Integer/lock, so no mutual exclusion at all
    void bad2() { synchronized (new Object()) { n++; } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Locking on a non-final field that gets reassigned (two threads lock two different objects).
  • Locking on interned Strings, boxed Integers (cached values are shared), or Class objects of shared libs.
  • Synchronizing the writer but not the reader; the reader then has no happens-before edge.
  • Believing synchronized on a method makes the whole class thread-safe; compound actions across two calls are still racy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is synchronized reentrant? → Yes, per-thread recursion count on the monitor.
  2. What happens to the lock if the body throws? → Released; the JVM generates an exception handler that runs monitorexit.
  3. Does synchronized guarantee fairness? → No. Waiting threads are not served FIFO; use a fair ReentrantLock if you need ordering (at a throughput cost).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer says "it locks the method". The senior answer names the lock object for each form, explains why exposing this as a lock is an encapsulation leak, and ties the lock to the memory-visibility guarantee.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service synchronized on an interned string key (synchronized(userId.intern())) to serialize per-user work; an unrelated library used the same literal and the two stalled each other.

questions.promptHtml: How do wait(), notify() and notifyAll() work? Why must wait() be called in a loop, and when is notify() not enough?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic low-level coordination primitive. Wrong usage causes lost wakeups and hangs, so it separates people who memorised the API from those who understand condition predicates.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: wait() must be called while holding the object's monitor. It releases that monitor, parks the thread in the object's wait set, and re-acquires the monitor before returning. notify wakes one waiter, notifyAll wakes all. I always wait inside a while (!condition) loop because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may have consumed the condition first. I default to notifyAll unless all waiters wait on the same single condition and any one can proceed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Thread A (consumer)                Thread B (producer)
synchronized(q){                   synchronized(q){
  while(q.isEmpty()) q.wait();       q.add(x);
  take();                            q.notifyAll();
}                                  }

Steps: A holds monitor, sees the empty queue, calls wait(): atomically releases monitor and joins the wait set. B takes the monitor, adds, calls notifyAll(): A moves from the wait set to the entry queue but cannot run until B exits the block. A then re-acquires the monitor, returns from wait() and must re-check the predicate.

Why the loop: (1) spurious wakeups are allowed by the spec; (2) with multiple consumers, a notified thread may find another consumer already took the item; (3) notifyAll wakes threads waiting for different conditions.

Why notify can hang: if producers and consumers share one monitor and notify() wakes another producer when the queue is full, the signal is "absorbed" and everyone ends up waiting. That is a lost wakeup in effect. Separate Conditions (see the Condition question) fix that cleanly.

Calling wait/notify without owning the monitor throws IllegalMonitorStateException. notify does not release the monitor; it happens only when the block exits. A notify issued before the waiter starts waiting is lost, which is why the predicate state must live in shared variables guarded by the same lock.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Box<T> {
    private T item;
    synchronized void put(T t) throws InterruptedException {
        while (item != null) wait();
        item = t;
        notifyAll();
    }
    synchronized T take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (item == null) wait();
        T t = item; item = null;
        notifyAll();
        return t;
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• if instead of while around wait().
  • Calling notify() when waiters wait on different predicates.
  • Setting no state flag: notify before wait is lost forever.
  • Swallowing InterruptedException and carrying on, which breaks cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Difference between sleep and wait? → sleep keeps held monitors and needs no lock; wait releases the monitor and requires owning it.
  2. Why are wait/notify defined on Object? → The monitor belongs to every object.
  3. What replaces this in modern code? → BlockingQueue, Condition, or higher-level utilities; raw wait/notify is rare outside JDK internals.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "wait waits, notify wakes". Senior: predicate-in-a-loop, why spurious wakeups are legal, lost signal scenarios, and why a single wait set is a design smell that Condition fixes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled bounded buffer used if plus notify; under load with 8 consumers one item would wake the wrong thread and pipeline stages stalled until a timeout retried.

questions.promptHtml: How does HotSpot implement synchronized under the hood? What are the lock states, and what happened to biased locking?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates repeat "synchronized is slow, so use Lock" from the Java 5 era. This checks whether you know the modern cost model and can reason about contention.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The lock state lives in the object's header (mark word). Uncontended locking is cheap and CAS-based ("thin"/lightweight). When threads actually contend, the JVM inflates to a heavyweight monitor (an ObjectMonitor) where losers spin briefly and then park. Biased locking, which optimised single-thread reuse, was disabled by default in JDK 15 (JEP 374) and deprecated for removal; I believe it was fully removed in a later release, so I'd verify the exact version. Today synchronized and ReentrantLock perform similarly in most workloads, so I choose on features, not on speed myths.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
unlocked  --CAS--> thin (lightweight) lock: owner recorded via stack lock record / mark word
thin      --contention--> inflated: ObjectMonitor (owner, entry list, wait set)
(historic) biased: mark word stores owner thread id, no CAS on re-entry; revoked at a safepoint if another thread wants it
  • Biased locking saved the CAS for objects locked repeatedly by one thread, but revocation was expensive (safepoint operations) and the code was invasive. JEP 374 states that benefits are much smaller on modern hardware and workloads, so it was switched off unless -XX:+UseBiasedLocking was given (JDK 15), and the flags were deprecated.
  • Inflated monitors: a contending thread spins adaptively before parking, avoiding a context switch when the owner releases quickly.
  • Newer JDKs reworked lightweight locking (the stack-locking scheme changed in recent releases); details are version-specific, so verify against your JDK release notes rather than assuming.
  • Object header size is relevant for memory (see the JVM memory chunk), and identityHashCode interacts with header bits, which is one reason lock-state transitions were intricate.

Practical consequences: (1) do not rewrite synchronized to Lock for "performance" without measuring; (2) contention, not lock choice, dominates latency; (3) -XX:-UseBiasedLocking advice in old blog posts is moot on modern JDKs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(diagnostic, not a fix)

# JDK 21+: see who is blocked on monitors
jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -A3 "waiting to lock"
# JFR event for contention
jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile
# look at jdk.JavaMonitorEnter / jdk.JavaMonitorWait events

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming synchronized always makes a kernel call. Uncontended cases do not.
  • Recommending -XX:+UseBiasedLocking on JDK 15+.
  • Saying "synchronized is slower than ReentrantLock" as a blanket rule.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is lock inflation? → Switching from thin to a full ObjectMonitor once contention or wait() occurs.
  2. Why did biased locking get removed? → Cost of revocation and maintenance vs shrinking benefit (JEP 374).
  3. How would you find monitor contention in prod? → JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, or async-profiler -e lock.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Java 6 added biased and lightweight locks". Senior: states the biased locking status with version, explains inflation triggers, and says measure with JFR before swapping lock types.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent a sprint replacing synchronized with ReentrantLock for speed and saw zero change; the real cost was a 400-thread convoy on one hot lock.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized? What do you give up?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A staple. It tests whether you can name concrete capabilities, not slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ReentrantLock gives me things synchronized can't: tryLock (optionally with a timeout), interruptible acquisition, optional fairness, multiple Conditions, and introspection like isLocked and getQueueLength. What I give up is automatic release: I must unlock() in a finally. If I need none of those features, I use synchronized because it can't leak a lock and is simpler.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Feature synchronized ReentrantLock
Release automatic on exit manual, finally
Try / timeout no tryLock(), tryLock(t,u)
Interruptible wait for lock no lockInterruptibly()
Fairness no new ReentrantLock(true)
Condition queues one wait set many Conditions
Scope block or method any code path, even across methods
Monitoring thread dump shows it also getOwner (protected), getQueueLength

Built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS): an int state (hold count) plus a CLH-style wait queue; blocked threads park via LockSupport. Reentrant: the owner increments the hold count; it must unlock the same number of times.

Memory semantics: same as monitors: unlock happens-before a subsequent lock of the same Lock.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

void update() {
    lock.lock();            // acquire BEFORE try
    try {
        // critical section
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();      // always release
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting lock() inside the try: if it throws, finally calls unlock() on a lock you don't hold (IllegalMonitorStateException masks the original).
  • Forgetting unlock on an early-return path.
  • Using lock.lock() plus wait(); use a Condition (await) instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it faster than synchronized? → Not materially in modern JDKs; choose on features.
  2. How do you know a thread holds it? → isHeldByCurrentThread().
  3. What is the AQS mental model? → State + FIFO queue of waiters; acquire tries CAS, else enqueues and parks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Lock is more flexible". Senior: lists concrete features, the finally discipline, AQS basics, and prefers synchronized when features are unused.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A forgotten unlock() on one early-return branch left a lock held forever; thread dumps showed 200 threads parked on one ReentrantLock with an owner that no longer existed in any task.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service caches rates and refreshes them with this code. After a deploy, once an upstream DB timeout began, the service logged IllegalMonitorStateException and then stopped serving rates: p99 went from 40 ms to timeouts, and a thread dump showed 150 threads WAITING on ReentrantLock$NonfairSync.

class RateCache {
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = Map.of();

    void refresh() {
        try {
            lock.lock();
            rates = loadFromDb();   // may throw on timeout
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }

    BigDecimal get(String k) {
        lock.lock();
        BigDecimal r = rates.get(k);
        if (r == null) return BigDecimal.ZERO;   // early return
        lock.unlock();
        return r;
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain the production symptoms, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap get in try/finally" only. It misses that lock() inside try is also wrong, that the lock is held while doing a slow DB call, and that readers are being serialised needlessly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often is refresh called, and is stale data acceptable? (decides whether to avoid locking readers). Is loadFromDb bounded by a timeout? What is the read RPS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart or roll back to drain the stuck lock; the owner never released it, so threads won't recover on their own.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) get leaks the lock on the null early return (each leaked hold count keeps it locked); (b) lock() inside try hides the original exception when lock() itself fails; (c) DB call under the lock stalls all readers during refresh; (d) red herring: connection pool, because the symptom is parked threads on a lock, not on socket reads.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print shows many threads parked on one lock object with an owner thread that is RUNNABLE or gone; grep logs for IllegalMonitorStateException; read the code for every exit path.
  5. Root cause: The get path returns without unlock when the key is missing; the reentrant hold count stays positive on that thread. If it is a pooled thread, it keeps the lock and other threads block forever. In refresh, a failure while acquiring leads finally to unlock an unheld lock.
  6. Fix: short-term: unlock in finally and move lock() before try. Long-term: do not lock readers at all.
private volatile Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = Map.of();

void refresh() {
    Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh = Map.copyOf(loadFromDb()); // slow work outside any lock
    rates = fresh;                                            // atomic publish via volatile
}
BigDecimal get(String k) { return rates.getOrDefault(k, BigDecimal.ZERO); }
  1. Prevention: Static analysis rule (Error Prone LockNotBeforeTry, SpotBugs), code review checklist: "every lock has lock(); try { } finally { unlock(); }", and a test that calls get for a missing key repeatedly from a pool.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add tryLock timeouts to paper over the leak. The immutable-snapshot design accepts brief staleness; if strict consistency is needed I'd use a read-write lock around a short critical section, not the DB call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if refresh must not run twice concurrently? → Use a tryLock() in refresh and skip if busy; readers stay lock-free.
  • Why does the leak only appear on a missing key? → The happy path unlocks; the early return is rare so tests missed it.
  • Would synchronized have avoided it? → Yes, automatic release; that is the case for it when you need no extra features.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a metrics cache locked on a rarely-taken error branch. It ran for months, then a partner sent an unknown key at 2 a.m. and the lock never released; the on-call restarted the pod three times before reading the code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds finally to one method; does not notice the DB call under the lock.
  • Hire: finds both lock-placement bugs, reads a thread dump correctly, fixes with try/finally.
  • Strong hire: also removes locking from the read path with an immutable snapshot, proposes lint rules and a regression test.

questions.promptHtml: What does a fair ReentrantLock do, and why isn't it the default? When would you pay for fairness?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of throughput vs starvation trade-offs, and of why "fair" is not a free upgrade.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A fair lock grants the lock to the longest-waiting thread; a non-fair one lets an arriving thread "barge" in if the lock happens to be free. Barging is faster because it avoids waking a parked thread and a context switch, so non-fair gives higher throughput. I use fair only when starvation is a real, observed problem or ordering is part of the requirement.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Non-fair: T4 arrives as owner releases -> CAS succeeds -> T4 runs; T1..T3 still parked
Fair:     T4 sees queued waiters -> enqueues behind T3; T1 is unparked and runs

In the fair mode, lock() checks hasQueuedPredecessors(); if someone is waiting it queues. The cost is that the next owner must be unparked (a wake-up latency of tens of microseconds or more) while the lock sits idle, so throughput drops, sometimes by an order of magnitude under contention in benchmarks (measure on your own hardware).

Caveats: the untimed tryLock() ignores fairness and barges even on a fair lock; the timed tryLock(t, unit) honours it. Fairness is about acquisition order only; it does not guarantee thread scheduling fairness. synchronized offers no fairness, and starvation under it is rarely seen in practice because of the barging plus adaptive spinning.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ReentrantLock fair = new ReentrantLock(true);
// fair.tryLock() would still barge; fair.tryLock(0, TimeUnit.SECONDS) would respect the queue

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Making every lock fair "to be safe".
  • Expecting fairness from tryLock().
  • Assuming a fair lock fixes starvation caused by long critical sections.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a thread starve on a non-fair lock? → In theory yes; in practice rare, and shortening the critical section is the better fix.
  2. Does the Semaphore support fairness? → Yes, a constructor flag; same trade-off.
  3. How would you prove fairness is needed? → Measure per-thread acquisition counts or max wait with JFR lock events; show a long tail attributable to barging.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "fair means FIFO". Senior: quantifies the throughput trade, mentions the tryLock loophole, and treats fairness as a last resort after shrinking the critical section.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team flipped an order-queue lock to fair to fix one slow consumer; throughput fell by about a third because each handoff now required a park/unpark.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Condition, and how does it improve on wait/notify? Show a bounded buffer.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you can build a correct blocking structure and understand why separate wait sets matter.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Condition is created from a Lock and gives that lock multiple independent wait sets. I use one condition for "not full" and another for "not empty", so a producer signals only consumers and vice versa, avoiding the wasted wakeups and lost-signal traps of a single wait set. The rules are the same as wait/notify: hold the lock, and always check the predicate in a loop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
lock.newCondition() returns a Condition; await() atomically releases the lock, parks, and re-acquires on wake; signal()/signalAll() move waiters from the condition queue to the lock queue. Also available: awaitNanos, await(time, unit) (returns false/remaining time on timeout), awaitUninterruptibly.

ReentrantLock
 |- notFull  condition queue : producers
 |- notEmpty condition queue : consumers

Why better: with one monitor, notify() might wake a producer when a consumer was needed. With two conditions, notEmpty.signal() can only wake a consumer, so signal() (not signalAll) is safe when exactly one waiter can proceed. Spurious wakeups are still permitted, so loop on the predicate. In practice you'd use ArrayBlockingQueue, which is implemented exactly this way.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private int head, tail, count;
    private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    BoundedBuffer(int cap) { items = new Object[cap]; }

    void put(T t) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();
            items[tail] = t; tail = (tail + 1) % items.length; count++;
            notEmpty.signal();
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == 0) notEmpty.await();
            T t = (T) items[head]; items[head] = null; head = (head + 1) % items.length; count--;
            notFull.signal();
            return t;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling await without holding the lock (IllegalMonitorStateException).
  • Using if instead of while.
  • Calling Object.wait() on a Condition object (compiles; wrong method).
  • Forgetting to null out the slot, which keeps a reference alive (a small leak).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just use ArrayBlockingQueue? → You should; build your own only to show the mechanism.
  2. signal vs signalAll? → signal is safe when any single waiter can proceed and all waiters wait on the same predicate.
  3. What happens if await is interrupted? → Throws InterruptedException after re-acquiring the lock.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Condition is like wait/notify for Lock". Senior: explains the two-queue split, lock re-acquisition on wake, timeout-return semantics, and recommends the library queue.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A home-grown job queue using one monitor and notify() hung when producers woke producers; moving to two conditions removed a nightly 20-minute stall.

questions.contextHtml: An order-matching API (800 RPS, 64 request threads on 8 vCPUs) updates a per-account balance under a ReentrantLock per account. A batch job occasionally holds a hot account's lock for ~4 s while recalculating. During it, request p99 climbs from 60 ms to 8 s, the thread pool saturates, the load balancer health check (2 s timeout) fails and pods are restarted, making things worse. Thread dump excerpt: 60 threads WAITING (parking) at ReentrantLock.lock(ReentrantLock.java). CPU is 15%.
questions.promptHtml: How do you stop the cascade, and how would you redesign the lock usage?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the thread pool" or "make the lock fair". More threads just means more parked threads; the lock is the bottleneck and CPU is idle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the batch job able to run off-peak or in chunks? Can requests for a locked account fail fast with a retryable error? What is the SLO for a single account's updates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause or throttle the batch job; temporarily remove the health check dependency on request threads (separate management thread); shed load for that account at the gateway.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) long critical section by the batch job, (b) request threads blocking unboundedly on lock(), (c) health check sharing the saturated pool, (d) red herring: GC, because CPU and heap were normal.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack/jcmd Thread.print to find the lock owner stack (the batch thread), JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter/park events or async-profiler -e lock for wait time, and Micrometer metrics for pool queue depth.
  5. Root cause: Unbounded blocking on a contended lock turns one slow holder into full thread-pool exhaustion. Idle CPU with parked threads is the signature.
  6. Fix: short-term: use tryLock with a timeout so requests fail fast.
if (!lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    throw new AccountBusyException(accountId); // map to 503 + Retry-After
}
try { applyDelta(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }

Long-term: shrink the batch's critical section (compute outside the lock, apply a quick delta inside), or use optimistic versioning on the row instead of a long in-memory lock; give batch work its own pool and lower priority. 7. Prevention: Alert on lock wait time and pool queue depth; load test with a slow lock holder (chaos test); code rule that no lock is held across I/O. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Timeouts convert latency into errors; clients need retries with jitter, and operations must be idempotent. I would not use lockInterruptibly alone: it only helps if something interrupts the waiters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why tryLock(timeout) and not plain tryLock()? → Plain tryLock() barges and fails immediately; a short timeout absorbs tiny contention bursts.
  • What if requests must never fail? → Queue per account (single-writer actor/serial executor) instead of locks.
  • Does a fair lock help? → No, the lock is held 4 s; ordering doesn't shorten it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite outage: a reconciliation job and live traffic shared a per-tenant lock. The fix was not a clever lock but moving the reconciliation to snapshot reads, shrinking the lock hold from seconds to microseconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales threads or restarts only.
  • Hire: identifies lock-owner via thread dump, applies tryLock timeout with proper error mapping.
  • Strong hire: separates pools, removes I/O from the critical section, adds lock-wait metrics and chaos test.

questions.contextHtml:
A config registry uses a ReentrantReadWriteLock. In staging all tests pass. In production, shortly after 20 threads began calling getOrLoad under traffic, the service hangs: no CPU, requests time out, and jstack shows threads WAITING in ReentrantReadWriteLock$WriteLock.lock, with the same threads also holding read locks.

private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
private final Map<String, Config> map = new HashMap<>();

Config getOrLoad(String key) {
    rw.readLock().lock();
    try {
        Config c = map.get(key);
        if (c == null) {
            rw.writeLock().lock();      // "upgrade"
            try {
                c = load(key);
                map.put(key, c);
            } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
        }
        return c;
    } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does it hang and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a ConcurrentHashMap" without explaining the deadlock, or "use fair mode".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is load slow or does it do I/O? Is it fine to load the same key twice? How many distinct keys?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart to clear the deadlock; temporarily route to an older build if the bug is new.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) read-to-write upgrade deadlock, (b) writer starvation, (c) the loader blocking on external I/O, (d) red herring: GC.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd Thread.print showing the same threads holding the read lock and waiting for the write lock; the JDK deadlock detector may not report it since it involves a lock owned by many readers, so inspect the "Locked ownable synchronizers" section.
  5. Root cause: ReentrantReadWriteLock does not support upgrading. A writer waits until all readers release. Two threads each hold a read lock and each requests the write lock, so each waits for the other to release its read lock: a deadlock. Even one thread alone can hang itself: the write lock cannot be taken while the same thread holds only the read lock.
  6. Fix: release read lock, take the write lock, then re-check (double-check pattern), or simply use ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (keep the loader short and non-recursive).
Config getOrLoad(String key) {
    Config c = map.get(key);                    // ConcurrentHashMap
    return (c != null) ? c : map.computeIfAbsent(key, this::load);
}
  1. Prevention: Review rule: "no write lock acquisition while holding a read lock"; a concurrency test with many threads and a cold cache.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: computeIfAbsent blocks other updates to the same bin during the load, so I'd keep load fast or use a Future-based memo for slow loads. I wouldn't add a timeout tryLock to hide the design bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is downgrading (write to read) allowed? → Yes: take the read lock while holding the write lock, then release write.
  • Why did staging pass? → Single-threaded or warm cache; the deadlock needs two threads missing simultaneously.
  • Would StampedLock help? → It offers tryConvertToWriteLock, which is conditional and may fail; the code still needs a fallback.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite hang: the "cache miss upgrade" path ran only after a deploy flushed the cache. The system was fine for weeks and froze on the first cold start under load.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain why threads wait.
  • Hire: states that upgrade is unsupported and fixes with release-then-write plus recheck.
  • Strong hire: replaces with ConcurrentHashMap or a future-based memo and discusses computeIfAbsent blocking caveats.

questions.promptHtml: What are the semantics of ReentrantReadWriteLock, and when does it actually help versus a plain lock?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates assume "many readers, one writer" is always a win. Seniors know the overhead, the starvation modes and the cases where it is slower.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Many threads can hold the read lock at once, but the write lock is exclusive and excludes readers. It helps when reads are frequent, the read critical section is long enough to amortise the lock's overhead, and writes are rare. It does not support upgrading read to write, supports downgrading, and under heavy read load writers can be delayed. For short read sections, an immutable snapshot, volatile, or a concurrent collection usually beats it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Built on AQS; the 32-bit state is split: upper 16 bits count shared (read) holds, lower 16 bits count exclusive (write) holds. Read-hold counts per thread are tracked separately (ThreadLocal-based, with a fast path for the first reader), which is a real overhead.
  • Rules: write lock is reentrant and may acquire the read lock (downgrade); a reader cannot acquire the write lock (deadlocks, see upgrade question).
  • Non-fair mode: ordering is unspecified, but a reader will not barge ahead if the head of the queue is a waiting writer (it avoids indefinite writer starvation in the common case). Fair mode: arrival order approximately.
  • The read lock does a CAS on shared state, so with many cores all readers hit the same cache line. Throughput can plateau, or even be worse than synchronized for tiny sections.
  • Conditions are only available on the write lock.
readers:  R1 R2 R3 -----+
writer:                  W waits until readers drain, blocks new readers when at head

When it helps: a read of 10-100 microseconds or more (parsing, scanning a structure), 90%+ reads. When not: reads of nanoseconds (field access, map get).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Downgrade: write -> read without a gap for other writers
rw.writeLock().lock();
try {
    update();
    rw.readLock().lock();   // acquire read before releasing write
} finally {
    rw.writeLock().unlock();
}
try { readUpdated(); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it around a HashMap.get and expecting a speedup.
  • Trying to upgrade read to write.
  • Assuming readers are unbounded and writers are safe from starvation in all modes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't it upgrade? → Two readers upgrading would each wait for the other's read hold: deadlock.
  2. Cheaper alternatives for read-mostly data? → Copy-on-write snapshot via volatile reference, CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap.
  3. What does StampedLock add? → Optimistic reads with no CAS write on shared state (separate question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "multiple readers, single writer". Senior: reasons from read duration and contention, names the cache-line cost, the starvation behaviour and the alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team wrapped a tiny cache lookup in a read lock and saw lower throughput than before at 32 cores, because all readers CASed the same state word.

questions.promptHtml: Explain StampedLock: optimistic reads, the three modes, and why it is dangerous to adopt casually.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most error-prone lock in java.util.concurrent. A senior should know both the performance idea and the sharp edges.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: StampedLock returns a long stamp for every acquisition. Besides write and read locks it offers an optimistic read: tryOptimisticRead() takes no lock at all, I read fields into locals, then validate(stamp) tells me whether a write happened in between. If validation fails I fall back to a real read lock. It is not reentrant, has no Conditions, and the optimistic path can observe inconsistent data until validated, so it needs careful code.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Modes: writing (exclusive), reading (shared), optimistic reading (no lock; just a version stamp). Optimistic read avoids writing to shared memory, so reads scale across cores far better than a CAS-based read lock.

long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead();   // 0 if write-locked right now
read fields into locals
if (!sl.validate(s)) {             // a writer intervened
    s = sl.readLock();             // fallback
    try { re-read fields } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); }
}

Rules from the Javadoc: reads between tryOptimisticRead and a successful validate may be inconsistent, so do not act on them (no using a half-read reference to dereference or loop) until validated; copy into locals first. Stamps can be converted (tryConvertToWriteLock, tryConvertToReadLock), which may fail and return 0; the caller must handle that.

Sharp edges:

  • Not reentrant: re-acquiring on the same thread blocks itself (deadlock).
  • Not tied to a thread: a stamp can be unlocked by another thread (rarely useful, easy to misuse).
  • No fairness choice and no Conditions.
  • Interruption: lock acquisition methods without Interruptibly ignore interrupts in a way that can leave threads busy-spinning a bit; use the ...Interruptibly variants for long waits.
  • Not a drop-in for ReentrantReadWriteLock; they have different failure modes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Point {
    private double x, y;
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

    double distanceFromOrigin() {
        long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
        double cx = x, cy = y;                 // copy to locals first
        if (!sl.validate(s)) {
            s = sl.readLock();
            try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); }
        }
        return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
    }

    void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long s = sl.writeLock();
        try { x += dx; y += dy; } finally { sl.unlockWrite(s); }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using optimistic reads of a reference, then dereferencing before validate.
  • Calling a method that takes the same StampedLock while holding it (self-deadlock).
  • Unlocking with the wrong stamp, or unlockRead on an optimistic stamp (illegal).
  • Using it with data not safe to read torn (e.g., long/double without care is fine under JMM because validate gives ordering, but multi-field invariants are the issue).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a tryOptimisticRead stamp a lock? → No; nothing to unlock.
  2. When is it worth it? → Very read-heavy, tiny read sections, many cores, measured gain.
  3. Why can invalid reads be dangerous? → You might compute a size from one field and index with another, causing an exception or infinite loop before validate catches it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "faster read-write lock". Senior: explains optimistic semantics, the locals-then-validate rule, non-reentrancy, and recommends it only after measurement showing the RW lock is the bottleneck.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A geometry service adopted StampedLock for a 3x read gain and later hit a self-deadlock when a refactor made a getter call another stamped method.

questions.contextHtml:
A 16-core market-data service holds a mutable Quote (bid, ask) in a StampedLock. Reads run at ~1.2M/s, writes ~2k/s. After a refactor, a rare ArithmeticException: / by zero and occasional negative spreads appear, about 5 per hour, and one pod hung with 3 threads WAITING on StampedLock.readLock.

class Quote {
    private double bid, ask;
    private int levels;
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

    double avgPerLevel() {
        long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
        double spread = ask - bid;
        double r = spread / levels;          // levels may be 0 transiently
        if (sl.validate(s)) return r;
        s = sl.readLock();
        try { return (ask - bid) / levels; } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); }
    }

    void update(double b, double a, int l) {
        long s = sl.writeLock();
        try { bid = b; ask = a; levels = l; refresh(); } finally { sl.unlockWrite(s); }
    }

    void refresh() {
        long s = sl.readLock();      // called inside update()
        try { /* recompute derived cache */ } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Identify every bug and describe the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "StampedLock is buggy, switch to synchronized." It misses the two concrete misuses: computing before validating and self-acquisition.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does levels ever legitimately equal 0? Is the read throughput actually needed (what did the previous lock cost)? Is refresh public?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the refactor that added refresh to the write path; guard the divide with a validated copy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) arithmetic on unvalidated optimistic reads; (b) update calls refresh, which takes the read lock while the same thread holds the write lock: StampedLock is not reentrant, so it blocks forever; (c) JIT reordering: red herring, since validate provides the needed ordering; (d) wrong stamp type on unlock.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dump: the hung thread is in update, parked in readLock under refresh (self-deadlock). For (a), a stress test with a writer flipping levels between 0 and 3 and many optimistic readers reproduces the exception in seconds.
  5. Root cause: Between tryOptimisticRead and validate, a writer may have partly applied an update (levels = 0 with the new bid), so the divide throws before the validation check runs. Separately, the non-reentrant lock deadlocks on the nested read.
  6. Fix:
double avgPerLevel() {
    long s = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
    double b = bid, a = ask; int l = levels;     // copy only
    if (!sl.validate(s)) {
        s = sl.readLock();
        try { b = bid; a = ask; l = levels; } finally { sl.unlockRead(s); }
    }
    return l == 0 ? 0 : (a - b) / l;            // compute after validated copy
}
void update(double b, double a, int l) {
    long s = sl.writeLock();
    try { bid = b; ask = a; levels = l; refreshLocked(); } // lock-free internal helper
    finally { sl.unlockWrite(s); }
}
  1. Prevention: Convention: optimistic section only copies fields; internal ...Locked helpers never lock; a jcstress or stress test; document that the class uses a non-reentrant lock.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't keep StampedLock if throughput measurements do not justify it; an immutable Quote record swapped through a volatile reference removes the whole class of bugs for a single allocation per write (2k/s is trivial).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would an immutable record be better here? → Yes: writes allocate an object, reads are a single volatile read, no validate logic.
  • Could the hung pod be a lost unlock? → Possible; the dump shows the owner stack, so check before guessing.
  • What if tryOptimisticRead returns 0? → A writer holds the lock; validate(0) returns false, so the fallback path runs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a pricing class was "optimised" with StampedLock, and weeks later a helper that was added for logging took the read lock inside a write section. It passed review because each method looked correct alone.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: misses both bugs.
  • Hire: finds compute-before-validate and the nested non-reentrant acquisition.
  • Strong hire: proposes the immutable-snapshot alternative, writes a stress test, and justifies when StampedLock is warranted.

questions.contextHtml: A rate-limiter service keeps per-API-key counters in a HashMap<String, Counter> guarded by one synchronized block. At 5k RPS on a 4-core pod it was fine (lock hold ~1 microsecond). Marketing expects 10x. In a load test at 40k RPS on 8 cores, throughput plateaus at ~18k RPS, CPU shows 35%, and async-profiler lock mode attributes 70% of wait time to that one monitor. There are ~200k distinct keys.
questions.promptHtml: How do you scale it, and what are the traps in each option?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ConcurrentHashMap" without understanding that the counter update must also be atomic, or "make the machine bigger", which does not help a single lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must counts be exact or approximate? What operations besides increment (reset windows, snapshots)? Is the key distribution skewed (a few hot keys)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add pods horizontally to cut per-pod RPS while I fix the structure, since the plateau is per-JVM.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) single global lock, hold time x arrival rate nearing saturation (utilisation approx. 40k x ~2us = 0.08 per lock, but cache-line transfers and parking inflate the real hold time); (b) hot keys making any striping uneven; (c) the counter objects themselves being contended; (d) red herring: GC, since allocation is small.
  4. How I'd verify each: async-profiler -e lock flame graph, JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter, a histogram of key frequency from logs, JMH test of candidate designs at 8 threads.
  5. Root cause: One monitor serialises all threads, and contention (parking, wake-ups, cache coherence) makes the effective service time several times the nominal 1 microsecond, so the lock saturates long before the CPU does.
  6. Fix: (1) Stripe: N independent locks selected by hash(key) & (N-1), N around 4x cores (a power of two, e.g. 32 or 64).
private final Object[] stripes = new Object[64];
{ for (int i = 0; i < stripes.length; i++) stripes[i] = new Object(); }
private final Map<String, long[]>[] shards; // one HashMap per stripe

void hit(String key) {
    int i = (key.hashCode() * 0x9E3779B9 >>> 26);   // top 6 bits of a mixed hash -> 0..63
    synchronized (stripes[i]) { shards[i].merge(key, new long[]{1}, (a, b) -> { a[0]++; return a; }); }
}

(2) Better: ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> with map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment() — CHM already locks per bin; LongAdder removes counter contention. Hot keys are then handled by cells in the adder. 7. Prevention: A JMH or k6 benchmark in CI at target concurrency; lock-wait SLO metric; dashboards on RPS per core. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Striping complicates operations that need global consistency (snapshot all counters, total size): you must take all locks in a fixed order. LongAdder.sum() is not an atomic snapshot, which is fine for rate limiting but not for billing. I wouldn't use ConcurrentHashMap.size() as a hot-path metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if one key gets 50% of traffic? → Striping by key does not help; use LongAdder or per-thread counters merged periodically, or shard the hot key.
  • Why a power of two? → Index by mask or shift, avoiding modulo, and a mixed hash avoids low-bit clustering.
  • Does the lock need to be reentrant? → Not for this design; keep the critical section a single map operation so no nesting occurs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite capacity test: a "tiny" global lock topped out the service at one third of the target. After striping, throughput scaled almost linearly until memory bandwidth became the limit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests bigger instances or more threads.
  • Hire: stripes or uses ConcurrentHashMap and notes atomic counter updates.
  • Strong hire: uses lock-profiling evidence, handles hot keys with LongAdder, and states what consistency is lost.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service transfers money between accounts. Each Account has its own ReentrantLock. At peak (1.5k transfers/s) the service periodically freezes: p99 jumps from 80 ms to timeouts, CPU drops to 5%, and jcmd Thread.print ends with "Found one Java-level deadlock" listing two request threads, each owning one account's lock and waiting for the other's.

void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amt) {
    from.lock.lock();
    try {
        to.lock.lock();
        try { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); }
        finally { to.lock.unlock(); }
    } finally { from.lock.unlock(); }
}

Thread A runs transfer(x, y) while thread B runs transfer(y, x). After the deadlock, subsequent requests touching x or y queue up, and the pool of 200 threads saturates in under 90 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the deadlock, fix it, and make it robust for 3+ accounts.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add timeouts" or "synchronize the whole method on a global lock". The first leaves wrong retries, the second serialises all transfers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can account IDs be compared (stable unique ID)? Are there transfers to self? Are multi-account operations (batch payouts) planned? What is the retry policy from clients?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart affected pods (a deadlock never self-heals); rate-limit or pause the offending flow; capture the thread dump first for evidence.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) circular wait from inconsistent lock order, confirmed by the JVM's deadlock report; (b) pool exhaustion as a consequence, not a cause; (c) red herrings: DB slowness and GC, since CPU is idle and the dump names the cycle.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print (look for "Found one Java-level deadlock", which covers monitors and ownable synchronizers like ReentrantLock), reproduce with two threads in a loop, ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() for in-process detection.
  5. Root cause: The four Coffman conditions held: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. The code created the cycle by acquiring locks in the order of the arguments rather than a global order.
  6. Fix: Impose a total order, e.g. by account ID, and acquire in that order.
void transfer(Account a, Account b, long amt) {
    Account first = a.id < b.id ? a : b;
    Account second = first == a ? b : a;
    first.lock.lock();
    try {
        second.lock.lock();
        try { a.debit(amt); b.credit(amt); }
        finally { second.lock.unlock(); }
    } finally { first.lock.unlock(); }
}

Handle a == b explicitly (reentrant lock tolerates it, but be explicit). For ties on a non-unique key, use a tie-breaker lock. Also consider tryLock with timeout and backoff as a defence in depth. 7. Prevention: A concurrency test hammering opposing transfers; a lint/review rule "acquire multiple locks only via LockOrdering helper"; production alert on ThreadMXBean deadlock detection; for the money path, prefer a DB transaction with ordered SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use a global lock (kills throughput), and I wouldn't rely on timeouts alone, because they create livelock-like retry storms when both sides back off the same way (use randomised backoff). In-memory locks protect only one JVM; with multiple pods the real source of truth must be the database.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the JVM detect deadlocks automatically? → It reports them in thread dumps; it does not break them.
  • What if IDs are not comparable? → Use System.identityHashCode with a global tie-break lock for collisions.
  • Why is this broken across pods? → The in-JVM lock does not exclude another pod; use row locks or optimistic versioning.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a deadlock appeared only when users sent each other money in the same second, so tests passed for a year. The thread-dump deadlock section took ten minutes to read; the fix was four lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot read the deadlock report or suggests only timeouts.
  • Hire: names circular wait, fixes with a consistent lock order.
  • Strong hire: handles self-transfer and ties, adds detection and tests, and points out multi-pod needs DB-level locking.

questions.promptHtml: What is a Semaphore, and how would you use it to bound concurrency to a downstream dependency?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the standard bulkhead tool, and the interviewer checks whether you understand permits (not ownership) and release discipline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Semaphore holds a count of permits. acquire takes one (blocking if none), release returns one. Unlike a lock, permits are not owned by a thread, so any thread can release. I use it to cap the number of concurrent calls to a limited resource, such as 20 in-flight calls to a payment provider. I always acquire before try and release in finally, and I prefer tryAcquire with a timeout so callers fail fast instead of piling up.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• AQS shared mode: state is the permit count; acquire CASes it down or queues; release CASes up and wakes waiters. Constructor new Semaphore(n, fair).
  • A binary semaphore (1 permit) resembles a lock but is not reentrant and not owner-checked: a second acquire by the same thread blocks itself.
  • Bounded concurrency vs bounded rate: a semaphore limits simultaneous work, not requests per second.
  • release without a matching acquire raises the permit count above the initial value (legal!), silently widening the limit. A common bug is releasing in finally when acquire failed or timed out.
  • With virtual threads, a Semaphore is the recommended way to cap concurrency to a scarce resource, instead of sizing a thread pool.
permits=3   [A][B][C] running ; D,E queued
A done -> release -> D acquires

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
private final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20);

Response call(Request r) throws InterruptedException {
    if (!permits.tryAcquire(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
        throw new OverloadedException();            // fail fast, nothing to release
    }
    try {
        return client.send(r);
    } finally {
        permits.release();                           // only reached after a successful acquire
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• acquire inside try with release in finally: if acquire is interrupted you release a permit you never had.
  • Treating it as a rate limiter.
  • Forgetting that permits are not tied to threads (async handoffs need an explicit release when the callback completes).
  • Using availablePermits() for decisions; it is a racy snapshot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Semaphore vs thread pool for limiting? → Pool bounds threads and queues work; semaphore bounds in-flight operations regardless of thread type.
  2. Fair or non-fair? → Fair for ordered admission, non-fair for throughput.
  3. How do you release in async code? → Release in the completion callback (whenComplete) on all paths including failure and cancellation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "controls access to a resource". Senior: acquire-outside-try discipline, permit inflation bug, fail-fast timeouts, and the async release problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leaked permit on an error path slowly reduced a 50-permit bulkhead to 0 over a week; the service degraded in steps until restart.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier? Give a use for each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic comparison; checks understanding of one-shot gates vs reusable rendezvous points.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CountDownLatch is a one-shot gate: threads call await() until the count reaches zero through countDown() calls, and it can't be reset. The counting threads and waiting threads can be different. CyclicBarrier makes a fixed set of N threads wait for each other at a rendezvous point; when the Nth arrives all are released, an optional barrier action runs, and the barrier resets for the next round.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CountDownLatch CyclicBarrier
Reusable No Yes (generations)
Who waits Anyone calling await The parties that call await, all of them
Who triggers countDown by any thread (a thread may call it many times) The Nth await
Failure mode countDown never reached: waiters hang One party interrupted/timed out: barrier "broken", others get BrokenBarrierException
Action none optional barrier action run by the last arriving thread

Uses: Latch: main waits for N services to finish starting, or a start gate that releases all workers simultaneously in a test (new CountDownLatch(1)). Barrier: iterative parallel algorithms where each phase needs all workers finished (simulation steps, parallel merge rounds).

Memory semantics: actions before countDown happen-before actions after a successful await return, so results written by workers are visible to the waiter.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) pool.execute(() -> {
    try { init(); } finally { ready.countDown(); }   // always count down
});
if (!ready.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) throw new IllegalStateException("startup timeout");

CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> mergeRound());
// each of 4 workers: do round; barrier.await(); do next round

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• countDown not in finally: an exception makes the waiter hang forever.
  • await() with no timeout in production code.
  • Expecting to reuse a latch.
  • Using more tasks than barrier parties on a small pool: threads waiting at the barrier occupy pool threads, so the remaining parties never run (pool deadlock).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a broken barrier? → If one waiting thread is interrupted, times out or the action throws, the barrier breaks and all other waiters get BrokenBarrierException.
  2. Can you add a party to a barrier? → No; use Phaser.
  3. Latch vs CompletableFuture.allOf? → Futures carry results/exceptions and compose without blocking; the latch is a blunt signal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "latch is one-time, barrier is reusable". Senior: adds failure modes (hang vs broken barrier), finally discipline, timeouts, and the pool-size deadlock with barrier parties.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup latch waited for 4 warmups; one warmup threw, never counted down, and the pod stayed "starting" until the orchestrator killed it, producing a crash loop.

questions.promptHtml: What does Phaser offer that CyclicBarrier and CountDownLatch don't? When would you reach for it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests breadth in the less-used utilities and the ability to say when a heavier tool is justified.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Phaser is a reusable barrier with a dynamic number of parties. Threads can register and deregister at any time, it tracks a phase number that advances each time all registered parties arrive, you can override onAdvance to run code at each phase and decide termination, and it supports arrive-without-waiting. It also supports a tree of phasers to reduce contention. I'd use it when the participant set changes over time, such as a recursive fork/join-style computation; for a fixed set of N workers, CyclicBarrier is simpler.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key methods: register(), bulkRegister(n), arriveAndAwaitAdvance() (like CyclicBarrier.await), arrive() (signal and continue), arriveAndDeregister() (leave), awaitAdvance(phase) (wait for a phase without being a party), getPhase(), isTerminated(). By default termination occurs when the number of registered parties drops to zero at a phase advance; you override onAdvance(phase, registeredParties) returning true to terminate (for example after N phases).

phase 0: parties {A,B,C} arrive -> onAdvance(0, 3) -> phase 1
A deregisters; D registers
phase 1: parties {B,C,D} ...

Differences:

  • Parties may vary; the barrier has fixed parties.
  • Phases are numbered, reusable indefinitely (the phase wraps at Integer.MAX_VALUE).
  • Termination replaces the "broken barrier" concept: after termination, waiting methods return immediately with a negative phase value.
  • Max 65535 registered parties per phaser (tiered phasers get around that).
  • Interruption of an arriveAndAwaitAdvance waiter does not break the phaser (the Javadoc contrasts this with CyclicBarrier); use awaitAdvanceInterruptibly when you need it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1) {                      // 1 = the main thread registers itself
    @Override protected boolean onAdvance(int phase, int parties) {
        return phase >= 2 || parties == 0;           // stop after 3 phases
    }
};
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    phaser.register();
    pool.execute(() -> {
        while (!phaser.isTerminated()) {
            doStep();
            phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();
        }
    });
}
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();                         // main leaves; workers keep going

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to deregister a failing party: the others wait forever (there is no broken-barrier safety net).
  • Registering after the phase has advanced and misreading which phase you joined.
  • Over-using it where a latch or barrier is enough.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you stop a phaser? → onAdvance returns true, or forceTermination().
  2. Why tiering? → To reduce CAS contention on one state word with many parties.
  3. Phaser vs structured concurrency / CompletableFuture? → For dynamic fan-out with result handling, futures or structured scopes are clearer; Phaser is for lock-step phases.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "like CyclicBarrier but more flexible". Senior: dynamic registration, phase and termination semantics, the absence of broken-barrier protection, and a clear criterion for choosing it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A parallel batch-loader used Phaser for variable worker counts; a worker that died of an exception never deregistered, stalling the batch until a try/finally with arriveAndDeregister was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A service starts 5 warm-up tasks (cache load, config fetch, JIT warmup requests, etc.) and blocks the readiness probe on a latch. Since a release on Tuesday, about 1 in 30 pod starts never becomes ready; the orchestrator kills them after 10 minutes and restarts them, making deployments take 40 minutes instead of 6. Logs show 4 tasks finishing; the fifth printed java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out once and then nothing. jstack shows main parked in CountDownLatch.await.

CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(5);
for (Runnable t : warmups) {
    pool.submit(() -> {
        t.run();               // may throw
        ready.countDown();
    });
}
ready.await();                 // readiness waits here
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. What else would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the readiness timeout." That hides the bug and ignores that submit swallows the exception into a Future nobody reads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the warm-up mandatory for correctness or just performance? What should happen if one fails: retry, start degraded, or fail the pod fast?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an await timeout and fail the pod fast so the orchestrator retries quickly; temporarily make the failing warm-up optional.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) task throws before countDown so the count never reaches zero; (b) submit hides the exception in the Future; (c) pool too small/deadlocked (red herring: 5 tasks on a 4-thread pool would show tasks never started, not a logged timeout); (d) network flakiness as the trigger, not the root cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dump shows main in await and pool threads idle (so not a pool deadlock); the one SocketTimeout log line identifies the task; check getCount() via debugger/logging equals 1.
  5. Root cause: countDown() is not in a finally, and submit swallowed the exception, so one transient error leaves the count at 1 forever. await() has no timeout, so nothing ever bounds it.
  6. Fix:
pool.execute(() -> {
    try { t.run(); }
    catch (Throwable e) { log.error("warmup failed", e); failed.set(true); }
    finally { ready.countDown(); }
});
if (!ready.await(2, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) throw new IllegalStateException("warmup timeout");
if (failed.get()) /* decide: retry, degrade, or fail fast */;

Or use CompletableFuture.allOf(...).orTimeout(2, MINUTES).join() so exceptions propagate naturally. 7. Prevention: Convention: every countDown in a finally; never await() without a timeout; a startup test that injects a failing warm-up; deployment metric for time-to-ready. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Starting degraded improves availability but may serve slow first requests; failing fast is safer if warm-up is required. I wouldn't raise the probe timeout, and I wouldn't ignore the failure silently.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a warm-up hangs rather than throws? → The timeout on await fires; also give each task its own timeout.
  • Why use execute rather than submit here? → execute routes uncaught exceptions to the thread's handler, but explicit catch is better still.
  • Could CyclicBarrier fit? → No; the waiter is not a party and we want one-shot semantics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident where a flaky dependency made 3% of deploys hang. The team lost days blaming the orchestrator before reading the code: one line, missing finally.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bumps timeouts.
  • Hire: finds the missing finally and adds a timeout.
  • Strong hire: also notes submit swallowing, decides failure policy with the product owner, and adds a failure-injection test.

questions.subtopic: synchronized vs ReentrantLock on virtual threads
questions.contextHtml: A team migrates a Tomcat/Spring service from a 200-thread platform pool to virtual threads on JDK 21, expecting to handle 5x concurrency. After canary at 20% traffic, throughput stalls near the old number, and p99 grows from 120 ms to 900 ms. CPU is 30%. JFR shows many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events with stack frames inside a vendor SDK's synchronized method that does a 150 ms blocking HTTP call. The DB pool (maximum 30) is not exhausted.
questions.promptHtml: Why is virtual-thread throughput capped, what do you do on JDK 21, and what changes on newer JDKs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Virtual threads are scalable so the issue must be the DB." This ignores pinning, which shows up directly in JFR.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which JDK build exactly (21 vs 24+)? Is the SDK source-modifiable or vendored? How many carrier threads (default is the number of cores)? What is the call rate through that SDK path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the canary back or cap the pinned call's concurrency; temporarily raise -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize (verify its effect and limits for your build) to compensate for pinned carriers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pinning: a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized keeps its carrier, and with 8 carriers on an 8-core pod only 8 such calls run at once; at 150 ms each that is about 8 / 0.15 s = ~53 calls/s, matching the stall; (b) native frames pinning (JNI); (c) DB pool limit (red herring: 30 connections were not exhausted); (d) something else saturating CPU (no, CPU was 30%).
  4. How I'd verify each: -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full on JDK 21 (verify flag behavior for your version), JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned with a threshold, and a thread dump via jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json.
  5. Root cause: On JDK 21, a virtual thread cannot unmount while it holds a monitor (synchronized) or runs a native frame. The blocking IO inside the synchronized method occupies the carrier thread, shrinking effective concurrency to the carrier count.
  6. Fix: short-term on 21: wrap the SDK call with a Semaphore to protect other work, or replace the synchronized with a ReentrantLock if the code is ours (a j.u.c lock lets the virtual thread unmount while waiting). For the vendor SDK, upgrade to a version that already uses ReentrantLock, or run that integration on a dedicated platform-thread executor. Long-term: JDK 24 (JEP 491) lets virtual threads block in synchronized without pinning their carrier; pinning still occurs for native frames, so keep monitoring the event.
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();   // instead of synchronized(this)
Response call(Req r) {
    lock.lock();
    try { return http.send(r); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
  1. Prevention: JFR pinned-thread alerts in canary, a load test at 5x concurrency before cutover, dependency audit for synchronized around blocking calls.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't blindly replace every synchronized with ReentrantLock; only those that guard blocking operations matter. Short, CPU-only synchronized sections are harmless. I also wouldn't push the carrier pool to hundreds of threads as a permanent fix; that recreates platform-thread limits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would moving to JDK 24+ alone fix it? → For monitor pinning, per JEP 491, yes; verify with JFR since native-frame pinning remains.
  • Does Object.wait() pin? → On 21 yes; JEP 491 also changed wait/notify on newer JDKs.
  • Why does a Semaphore help? → It bounds in-flight calls and, being j.u.c, lets waiting virtual threads unmount.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration: the canary looked healthy on CPU yet flat on throughput. A single pinned-thread event stack pointed to a third-party client; vendoring a patched build restored the expected scaling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames DB or says "virtual threads don't work".
  • Hire: identifies pinning from JFR, explains carrier limit, proposes lock replacement.
  • Strong hire: does the throughput math, knows the JDK 24 change, and sets up canary pinning alerts and bounded fallbacks.

questions.promptHtml: You need to coordinate threads: how do you decide between synchronized, ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock/StampedLock, Semaphore, latches/barriers, and higher-level structures? Walk me through your decision process.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The senior signal is judgement: choosing the simplest correct primitive and justifying it with data, not reciting API trivia.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start by asking whether I need shared mutable state at all; immutable data, confinement, or a concurrent collection often removes the lock. If I do need mutual exclusion, I use synchronized by default for simplicity and move to ReentrantLock only for tryLock, interruptibility, fairness or multiple conditions. Read-write locks and StampedLock come only after profiling shows read contention on long-enough read sections. Semaphores bound concurrency, latches signal one-time events, barriers and phasers synchronise rounds. And for handoff between threads I prefer a BlockingQueue over hand-built wait/notify.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision table:

Need Tool
Atomic compound update on a few fields synchronized or AtomicXxx/LongAdder for a single counter
Try/timeout/interrupt while acquiring ReentrantLock.tryLock / lockInterruptibly
Multiple wait conditions ReentrantLock + Conditions
Read-mostly, long reads ReentrantReadWriteLock; extreme read-heavy and tiny: immutable snapshot or StampedLock (careful)
Cap in-flight operations Semaphore
Wait for N events once CountDownLatch (or CompletableFuture.allOf)
N threads rendezvous each round CyclicBarrier; dynamic membership: Phaser
Producer-consumer BlockingQueue
Per-key mutual exclusion at scale striped locks or ConcurrentHashMap.compute
Many blocking tasks on JDK 21+ virtual threads plus Semaphore; avoid pinning locks

Principles: (1) smallest critical section, never hold a lock across I/O or an unknown callback; (2) consistent lock ordering when taking several; (3) prefer designs that remove sharing: confinement, message passing, snapshots; (4) measure with lock profiling (async-profiler -e lock, JFR monitor events) before adopting a more complex lock; (5) always bound waiting with timeouts at system boundaries.

Failure-mode lens: synchronized cannot leak a lock; Lock can; Semaphore permits can inflate; latches hang if not counted down; barriers break; StampedLock self-deadlocks on reentry.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Default: simple and safe
synchronized (this) { balance += delta; }

// Needs timeout -> ReentrantLock
if (lock.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    try { work(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing the most sophisticated lock first (premature optimisation).
  • Holding a lock during a network call.
  • Mixing multiple primitives for one invariant, which makes reasoning impossible.
  • Skipping the question "does this state need to be shared?".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Your read-heavy cache is slow under a RW lock; next steps? → Check read section length and core count; try an immutable snapshot or ConcurrentHashMap; consider StampedLock only with a benchmark.
  2. How would you test the choice? → JMH at realistic thread counts plus a stress test; contention profile in staging.
  3. When is a lock the wrong tool entirely? → When an actor/queue per entity or a DB transaction gives simpler single-writer semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names each primitive's definition. Senior: leads with eliminating sharing, defaults to the simplest primitive, cites failure modes and measurement, and knows the virtual-thread implications.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team layered RW locks, semaphores and a custom barrier around one cache; a single refactor to an immutable snapshot plus a bounded queue cut code by 400 lines and removed three recurring hangs.
